chapter_title: The Chapter of the Four Kingdoms
chapter_note: This chapter contains NO cosmological-correspondential substrate. Teaching purity is 0.000. The entire chapter is a Manichaean homiletic composition: Mani takes a Jesus saying (Matt 10:42) about giving a cup of water, lists four contemporary political kingdoms (Babylon/Persia, Rome, Axumites, Silis) as a rhetorical foil, and argues that alms-giving to disciples and catechumens surpasses worldly greatness. The 'four kingdoms' are earthly political entities, not cosmic domains — no degree mapping, no correspondential structure. Every paragraph either frames, cites scripture, applies to church categories, or exhorts. Gardner notes the unusual reference to the Holy Spirit rather than the Light Mind, confirming this is a distinctively Manichaean ecclesiastical composition rather than transmitted older teaching.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic opening 'Once again the apostle speaks' followed by a topic statement about earthly political kingdoms. 'Four great kingdoms in the world' refers to contemporary political entities, not cosmic domains — no substrate cosmological content to extract.

Lists four contemporary political kingdoms: Babylon/Persia, Romans, Axumites, Silis. These are historical-geographical references from Mani's world — the editor's contemporary political landscape. No cosmic correspondences or degree mappings. Silis is likely China (Serica); the four represent the known world's great empires. This is institutional context-setting, not cosmological substrate.

First-person Mani voice ('I, I say to you in truth') echoing/paraphrasing Jesus' saying about giving bread and water to disciples. Compares this to the four kingdoms. Institutional moral teaching about alms-giving to the community. 'My disciples', 'God's truth', 'righteousness' — all community-oriented. No cosmological-correspondential content.

Editorial seam correctly detected. 'Not only this, but whoever will give bread and a cup of water to a catechumen' — extends the preceding teaching to the catechumenate. Explicitly institutional vocabulary (catechumen, truth). Eschatological promise ('rest for ever') is characteristic of institutional/exhortatory layer.

Explicit NT citation formula: 'Just as the saying that the good saviour uttered.' This is the clearest marker of late composition — the substrate expounds, it does not cite. Paraphrases Matthew 10:42 / Mark 9:41 about giving water to 'the least of the faithful.' The oldest teaching layer never cites external scripture.

Hermeneutical interpretation of Jesus' saying: 'the saviour is calling these saints least of the faithful.' Then first-person Mani applies this to catechumens: 'I have proclaimed of the catechumens.' Heavy institutional vocabulary (catechumens, knowledge, kingdoms, truth of God, lust of the world, livelihood). This is scriptural exegesis applied to church categories.

Editorial seam correctly detected. 'Indeed, due to this, I tell you' — bridge connective with first-person address. Names church categories explicitly: 'faithful catechumen' and 'faithful righteous one.' Reference to Holy Spirit dwelling in them. Gardner notes this is unusual (Holy Spirit rather than Light Mind), suggesting a distinctively Manichaean composition layer.

Institutional theology of alms-giving: fellowship, Holy Spirit indwelling, thanksgiving before the Father, reward at the last day. Trinitarian-adjacent structure (Holy Spirit → true Father → reward). Entirely ecclesiastical — describes the mechanics of religious merit through community practice.

Devotional closure with near-beatitude formula: 'Blessed are these who will hear and believe it, and set their heart upon it.' First-person retrospective ('I have unveiled for you', 'I have told you'). Classic exhortatory wrapper closing a teaching sequence. 'Single mind' echoes community devotional language.
